items.examiner_comment: The text must be written entirely in the past tense.
items.response: We respectfully disagree. In computer science writing, tense follows function rather than a single rule: the present tense is conventionally used for definitions, established methods, descriptions of the proposed framework, and the reporting of results as they appear in tables and figures, while the past tense is used for one-off procedures such as data collection and training. Converting the entire text to the past tense would incorrectly imply that established methods and definitions no longer hold. We have, however, reviewed the text and corrected passages where tense was used inconsistently.
items.change_made: No change of convention. Passages that mixed tenses within a section were corrected throughout Chapters 1, 4, 5 and 6.
items.quote_from_text: Several passages mixed tenses within the same section. For example, results were reported in the past tense (“HyPER achieved the highest success rate…”) alongside present-tense analysis. Likewise, one-off procedures appeared in the present tense (“the dataset… is partitioned”).
items.revised_text_fix: The framework, contributions and results now consistently use the present tense (e.g., “HyPER achieves the highest success rate…”). One-off procedures such as data collection, training and running the experiments use the past tense (e.g., “the dataset… was partitioned”). Proposed future work uses the conditional (e.g., “future work could explore…”).

items.revised_text_fix: HyPER rests on three contributions. First, an automated geometric labelling pipeline produces dense risk labels from surface normals without manual annotation. Second, an adaptation of RandLA-Net predicts point-wise risk directly from raw 3D point clouds; used alone, it outperforms STEP on irregular terrain (65% versus 20% success in the Uneven environment) but is unreliable at drop-offs. Third, a confidence-aware fusion algorithm weights each branch by its confidence and penalises uncertainty. Combined with the visibility-aware occlusion handling and the local exploration strategy, HyPER achieves the highest overall success rate (60.8%) and the lowest mean collision count of the four frameworks, and it is the most consistent framework across hazard types. In the Cliff environment, it is the only framework that both ascends the ramp and avoids the cliff edge, re-planning safely in 19 of 20 runs.

items.examiner_comment: The 51 classes used to categorise risk in the RandLA-Net method seem to be too many, given the results in Figure 5.1. In retrospect, would a smaller range of values be as good as, or better at, prediction?
items.response: We agree that the per-class results in Figure 5.1 are weak, and that fewer classes would very likely increase mIoU. Classification accuracy is not, however, the purpose of the RandLA-Net branch in HyPER: it supplies a graded risk estimate on the same 0–50 scale as the geometric branch, so that the two can be fused cell by cell and the planner can trade off terrain of different risk. A coarse scale would quantise this estimate, and a binary scale would reduce it to an obstacle map. The fine scale does have costs: many classes have few training points, and probability spread over neighbouring classes lowers the entropy-based confidence used in the fusion. We have added this discussion to Section 5.1, noting that in retrospect an intermediate resolution may balance these better, and added a comparison of resolutions to Future Work.
items.change_made: Added a discussion of class resolution at the end of Section 5.1. Added an ablation paragraph at the end of Future Work (Section 6.2), which also covers comments 4 and 5.

(2) (No existing text replaced — new text inserted before the references, i.e. at the end of Section 6.2 (Future Work).)
items.revised_text_fix:
(1) The class-wise IoU in Figure 5.1 raises the question of whether a coarser risk scale would predict better. Fewer classes would almost certainly increase mIoU, since each class would contain more training points, and a binary safe/unsafe labelling would be the easiest to classify. Classification accuracy is not, however, the purpose of the RandLA-Net branch. Its role in HyPER is to supply a graded risk estimate on the same 0–50 scale as the geometric branch, so that the two can be fused cell by cell according to their confidence, and so that the planner can trade off terrain of different risk rather than only avoid terrain labelled unsafe. A coarse scale would quantise this estimate, and a binary scale would reduce the learned branch to an obstacle map that cannot distinguish a gentle slope from a moderate one.

The fine scale nevertheless has two costs. First, dividing the slope range into 50 steps leaves few training points in many classes, so resolving all 51 levels reliably requires more, and more balanced, training data. Second, because the RandLA-Net confidence is derived from the normalised entropy of the softmax output (Equations 3.5 and 3.6), probability spread over adjacent classes lowers R_C even when the prediction is close to the true risk. The choice of resolution is therefore a trade-off between the detail of the risk estimate and the data needed to learn it, and an intermediate resolution or an ordinal formulation may balance it better for our dataset. We identify a systematic comparison of resolutions as future work (Section 6.2).

(2) Two ablation studies would further clarify the contribution of individual design choices. First, we propose varying the resolution of the learned risk scale, comparing the 51-class scheme with coarser schemes (for example 2, 5 or 10 classes) and with an ordinal formulation, evaluated on downstream navigation performance and ordinal prediction error rather than on mIoU alone. Second, we propose applying the visibility-aware occlusion handling and the local exploration strategy to the baseline frameworks, or removing them from HyPER, while logging each activation of the exploration strategy, so that the effect of the confidence-aware fusion can be separated from that of the other HyPER components (Section 4.4).

items.examiner_comment: Section 3.3.2 (Local Exploration Strategy): given all the safety checks built into HyPER, it seems the algorithm could easily fail to offer any meaningful path to the goal, triggering the exploration strategy. How often did this occur in the experiments, and was it significant to the success of HyPER?
items.response: By design, the strategy is triggered only when the goal cell itself is classified as high risk, so it does not intervene when the goal region is observed as low risk. Its clearest effect is in the Obstacles Ramp environment, where it delays the ascent of the only viable ramp and lowers HyPER's success rate there (40%, compared with 75% for Simple Fusion). It is therefore significant to HyPER's results: it prevents deadlock when the goal region is temporarily classified as high risk, at the cost of longer runs where the direct route is traversable. We have added a paragraph to Section 5.3 discussing this, and logging of its activations is part of the ablation proposed in Future Work.
items.change_made: Added a paragraph to the Obstacles Ramp analysis in Section 5.3 on the effect of the exploration strategy. Activation logging is part of the ablation added to Future Work (see comment 3).

items.revised_text_fix: The local exploration strategy (Section 3.3.2) is triggered only when the goal cell itself is classified as high risk, so it does not intervene when the goal region is observed as low risk. In the Obstacles Ramp environment, its effect is clearly visible: exploration delays the ascent of the only viable ramp (Figure 5.15), which lowers HyPER's success rate there (40%, compared with 75% for Simple Fusion). The strategy is therefore significant to HyPER's results: it prevents deadlock when the goal region is temporarily classified as high risk, at the cost of longer runs where the direct route is in fact traversable. items.examiner_comment: It would be interesting to see how the results from the simulated environment translate to actual real-world environments with physical robots. If such experiments were attempted, some discussion would be nice; if not, some mention of the challenges involved could be given.
items.response: We agree. We do not attempt experiments with a physical robot in this work, and we now state this explicitly. Following the examiner's suggestion, we expand the Future Work section to discuss the main challenges of real-world deployment.
items.change_made: Rewrote the third paragraph of Section 6.2 to discuss the challenges of real-world deployment.
items.quote_from_text: All experiments in this dissertation are conducted within high-fidelity simulations using Cosys-AirSim and UE5. While the physics engine accurately models rigid-body dynamics and sensor noise, real-world deployment introduces additional challenges that simulations cannot fully replicate, including dust occlusion, surface reflectivity variation, and LiDAR beam divergence on wet or irregular rock surfaces. Future work evaluates HyPER on a physical Clearpath Husky platform within a controlled underground test environment. Domain randomisation techniques applied during training, such as stochastically varying point cloud density, adding structured noise, and simulating partial sensor occlusion, improve the robustness of the RandLA-Net component under real sensor conditions. Furthermore, online adaptation of the confidence thresholds in the fusion equation based on observed sensor quality metrics allows the system to self-calibrate when deployed in previously unseen environments.
items.revised_text_fix: We conducted all experiments in simulation using Cosys-AirSim and UE5 and did not attempt experiments with a physical robot. Transferring HyPER to a physical platform raises several challenges that our simulation does not capture. A physical LiDAR returns noisier data, with missing returns from wet or dark rock and spurious returns from dust, so RandLA-Net, trained only on clean simulated clouds, would face a distribution shift. Odometry drift in GPS-denied tunnels would misalign the accumulated scans and create artificial steps in the elevation grid. On real rock, the skid-steer Husky's turning depends on wheel slip and friction, which the kinematic bicycle model used by our NMPC does not capture and the simulation models only approximately; an embedded computer would slow the risk-map update rate, and measuring tip-over rates safely would require tethers, remote emergency stops and a purpose-built test area. Future work could therefore evaluate HyPER on a physical Clearpath Husky in a controlled underground test environment. Domain randomisation during training, such as varying point density, adding structured noise and simulating partial occlusion, could improve the robustness of RandLA-Net to real sensor data, and the confidence thresholds of the fusion equation could be adapted online to the observed sensor quality.

items.response: We agree. The review already covers approaches from the DARPA SubT Challenge (Section 2.3.1), including learning-based exploration policies and STEP and its extensions. We have broadened this with a paragraph on early mine-mapping robots, traversability in the SubT finalist systems and negative obstacle detection, which relates directly to HyPER's occlusion handling.

items.quote_from_text: (No existing text replaced — new paragraph inserted after the paragraph ending '…based on the estimated traversability cost and exploration volume.')
items.revised_text_fix: Beyond learning-based exploration, underground robotics has a longer history in mining. Thrun et al. [2004] deploy a wheeled robot to autonomously map abandoned mines, identifying challenges that still define the field: the absence of GPS, poor lighting, loss of communication and terrain that cannot be traversed safely. In the DARPA SubT Challenge, the finalist teams relied on LiDAR-based traversability assessment within complete autonomy stacks, for example combining legged and aerial robots with graph-based exploration on volumetric maps [Tranzatto et al. 2022] or deploying heterogeneous robot teams with a shared LiDAR-based navigation stack [Hudson et al. 2021], and a single misjudged drop-off or slope could end a robot's mission [Chung et al. 2023]. Negative obstacles are particularly difficult to perceive because they produce few or no LiDAR returns. Heckman et al. [2007] infer them by reasoning about occluded regions, an idea closely related to the visibility-aware occlusion handling in HyPER, and Hines et al. [2020] represent occluded regions with virtual surfaces, so that a robot approaches a potential drop cautiously until it is resolved as either a traversable slope or a fatal edge.

Tranzatto et al. and Chung et al. are already cited. The bib entry for hines2021virtual has year 2020, which matches the text here and in comment 6.

items.examiner_comment: Aggregated mIoU seems like the wrong metric for performance here, especially given its low performance on this task (the best class, class 1, is at 27%, i.e. less than 1 in 3 correct). This should prompt further investigation, as the metric is delinked from navigation performance.
items.response: We agree that mIoU alone is a limited measure here. With 51 ordinal classes of 1.4° each, a prediction one class from its label counts as entirely wrong, so exact-match accuracy is low even when predictions are close to the true risk. We have stated this limitation in Section 4.2.1, removed the claim that the model is 'highly effective', and explained in Section 5.1 why segmentation accuracy is only loosely linked to navigation: predictions are averaged per grid cell and smoothed by the CVaR before planning, and the labels themselves come from a slope heuristic. The navigation results remain our primary evaluation, and they support HyPER's design of weighting RandLA-Net by its confidence rather than using it alone.
items.change_made: Added a sentence on the limitation of mIoU to Section 4.2.1. Rewrote the per-class analysis and closing discussion in Section 5.1 and corrected the Figure 5.1 caption.
items.quote_from_text:
(1) This metric provides a granular view of how well the network distinguishes between various risk levels, such as safe flat ground versus critical cliff edges.

(2) A deeper examination of individual class performance reveals that the model is highly effective in the areas most critical for navigation.

(3) As shown in Figure 5.1, a deeper examination of individual class performance reveals that the model is highly effective in the regions most critical for autonomous navigation. The network achieves its highest accuracy at the extremes of the risk spectrum: approximately 27% IoU for class 1 and 11% for class 49. The lower performance across intermediate labels is largely an artifact of the evaluation metric treating all classes independently, rather than an indication of poor navigational capability.
A critically important observation is that classes 0, 1, 16, 26, 36, 37, and 49 achieve notably higher mIoU than the surrounding classes. These "anchor classes" effectively partition the continuous risk spectrum into operationally distinct zones:
• Safety Identification: High accuracy on classes 0 and 1 ensures the model confidently identifies traversable terrain, preventing the planner from unnecessarily avoiding benign surfaces.
• Hazard Detection: The strong performance on class 49 confirms that the network can detect near-critical hazards with sufficient reliability to trigger avoidance behaviour.
• Transitional Thresholds: Elevated accuracy on intermediate classes (16, 26, 36, and 37) suggests the model has learned to recognise key boundaries, such as the transition from moderate slopes to steep, unstable gradients, that correspond to meaningful changes in the robot's physical stability.

(4) These results imply that when the model is deployed within the full navigation pipeline, it reliably distinguishes between the risk categories that matter most for safe trajectory planning. Therefore, while the aggregate mIoU is numerically low, it does not directly translate to poor navigational capability. The practical effectiveness of RandLA-Net must be evaluated within the complete autonomous navigation pipeline rather than judged solely on isolated segmentation metrics.

(5) Figure 5.1 caption: "Class-wise IoU performance for the RandLA-Net model. The results show high accuracy on critical classes like class 0 and class 50 (representing the safest and riskiest labels), but low accuracy on the intermediate labels."
items.revised_text_fix:
(1) Because the 51 risk classes are ordinal (class 30 is closer to class 31 than to class 0), mIoU treats a prediction one class away from the label as an error of the same severity as a prediction at the opposite end of the scale. We report mIoU for comparability with the semantic segmentation literature, but it measures only exact agreement with the slope-based labels, so the navigation metrics in the following sections remain our primary basis of evaluation.

(2) (Sentence deleted.)

(3) Figure 5.1 shows the IoU of each individual class. The highest values occur at the extremes of the risk spectrum, approximately 27% for class 1 and 11% for class 49, with local peaks at classes 0, 16, 26, 36 and 37. For context, a uniform random guess over 51 classes would be correct for only about 2% of points. The peaks likely correspond to slope angles that occur frequently in our training environments, such as level ground, the ramp inclines and vertical faces, so they provide a coarse partition of the risk spectrum:

• Near-level terrain (classes 0–1): the most reliably identified region, which allows benign surfaces to be recognised.

• Near-maximum risk (class 49): identified less reliably, which is why HyPER does not rely on RandLA-Net alone to detect severe hazards.

• Intermediate peaks (classes 16, 26, 36 and 37): these reflect slope regimes present in the training ramps.

(4) The segmentation metrics are only loosely linked to navigation performance, for two reasons. First, we aggregate the per-point predictions before planning: we average them within each 0.1 m grid cell (Section 3.2) and smooth them with the neighbourhood CVaR, so that point-level confusion between adjacent classes largely averages out. Second, our labels come from the geometric labelling pipeline, so agreement with them measures how closely RandLA-Net reproduces a slope-based heuristic rather than how well it predicts physical traversability. Used on its own, RandLA-Net achieves the lowest overall success rate of the four frameworks (Table 5.1), which supports the central design decision of HyPER: to weight RandLA-Net predictions by their entropy-based confidence and combine them with the geometric branch.

(5) "Class-wise IoU of RandLA-Net on the validation trajectories."

items.examiner_comment: The argument for using the simulator for navigation performance is well founded; however, the risk map assessment, which is the novel part of this work, could have been evaluated on benchmarkable data. The simulations are not specifically subterranean, so this would give more insight into performance.
items.response: We thank the examiner for this point. Our validation scenarios deliberately isolate the geometric hazards that characterise subterranean terrain (uneven floors, steep slopes, cliffs and pits), since a risk assessment method must first handle each of these reliably; we now state this scope in Section 4.1.2 and in the abstract. No public dataset provides risk labels comparable to ours, because risk depends on the platform's physical limits, and relabelling a real dataset such as SubT-MRS with our pipeline would test sim-to-real transfer rather than the quality of the risk map. We therefore evaluate the risk map through closed-loop navigation outcomes and identify evaluation on real data as future work.

items.revised_text_fix:
(1) We designed these validation scenarios to isolate the geometric hazards that characterise subterranean terrain, namely irregular floors, steep inclines, cliff edges and pits, rather than to reproduce complete underground environments. A risk assessment method must first handle each of these hazards reliably, and testing them in isolation makes each failure attributable to a specific hazard. Our results therefore characterise HyPER's response to subterranean hazard types and provide the foundation for evaluation in complete underground environments, with enclosing walls and ceilings, narrow branching passages, dust and water. Public LiDAR datasets such as SubT-MRS [Zhao et al. 2024] and RELLIS-3D [Jiang et al. 2021] provide real point clouds, but none provides risk labels in our 0–50 scheme, because risk is defined relative to the physical limits of a specific platform. Applying our labelling pipeline (Section 4.3.2) to these datasets would measure how closely RandLA-Net reproduces the slope-based heuristic on real data, which tests sim-to-real transfer rather than the quality of the risk map itself. We therefore evaluate the risk maps through closed-loop navigation outcomes and identify evaluation on real data as future work (Section 6.2).

(2) We evaluate the proposed system in high-fidelity, physics-based simulations in Unreal Engine 5, across six scenarios that reproduce geometric hazards characteristic of subterranean environments, namely uneven ground, steep ramps, cliffs and pits, at varying levels of difficulty.

(2) Experimental results demonstrate that HyPER outperforms standalone baseline methods in navigation success, collision reduction, and platform stability. Ultimately, the fused risk map generates more conservative, geometrically accurate path trajectories, significantly reducing terminal failures in complex environments where safe exploration is critical.

(3) Comparative experiments demonstrate that HyPER outperforms the baseline STEP framework in complex terrains, specifically in the detection of negative obstacles such as cliffs, significantly reducing the rate of catastrophic failure while maintaining a high success rate in autonomous navigation tasks.
items.revised_text_fix:
(1) [New section: Overall Performance for Subterranean Navigation]

The per-scenario analysis shows how each framework responds to individual hazards, but for the subterranean use case we interpret the scenarios together, grouped by the type of hazard they represent. Table 5.9 groups the six scenarios into four hazard categories and reports success rates with 95% Wilson confidence intervals. It also reports the number of runs that end in a tip-over, which is the most consequential failure in an underground deployment because the robot usually cannot be recovered.

[Table 5.9: Success rate (%) with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and tip-over counts, grouped by hazard category.]
Hazard category | Scenarios (runs) | STEP | RandLA-Net | STEP + RandLA-Net | HyPER
Obstacles on level ground | Normal (20) | 90.0 [69.9, 97.2] | 95.0 [76.4, 99.1] | 95.0 [76.4, 99.1] | 100.0 [83.9, 100.0]
Irregular terrain | Uneven (20) | 20.0 [8.1, 41.6] | 65.0 [43.3, 81.9] | 90.0 [69.9, 97.2] | 70.0 [48.1, 85.5]
Slopes | Multi-Ramp, Obstacles Ramp (40) | 12.5 [5.5, 26.1] | 12.5 [5.5, 26.1] | 62.5 [47.0, 75.8] | 50.0 [35.2, 64.8]
Negative obstacles | Cliff, Hole (40) | 47.5 [32.9, 62.5] | 10.0 [4.0, 23.1] | 0.0 [0.0, 8.8] | 47.5 [32.9, 62.5]
Lowest category success | | 12.5 | 10.0 | 0.0 | 47.5
Tip-overs, all scenarios | (120) | 20 | 30 | 33 | 23
Tip-overs, excluding Hole | (100) | 1 | 11 | 15 | 7

Three observations summarise HyPER's performance for the subterranean use case. First, HyPER is the most consistent framework across hazard categories: its lowest category success rate (47.5%, for negative obstacles) is far higher than that of any baseline. Each baseline fails almost completely in at least one category: STEP on slopes (12.5%), RandLA-Net on slopes and negative obstacles (12.5% and 10.0%), and Simple Fusion on negative obstacles, where it does not complete a single run. In a subterranean mission, where the sequence of hazards is not known in advance, this consistency matters more than the best performance in any single category. Second, HyPER's advantage over Simple Fusion (Section 5.3) comes from the type of failure it avoids: Simple Fusion drives off the cliff edge in 12 of 20 Cliff runs, whereas HyPER does so in none. Third, STEP records the fewest tip-overs (20 of 120) largely because it does not attempt to climb slopes, which also explains its low success rate; HyPER's 7 tip-overs outside the Hole all occur in the Obstacles Ramp environment. Overall, HyPER is the only evaluated framework without a near-complete failure in any hazard category, which makes it the most dependable choice when the hazards ahead are unknown, while pit-type negative obstacles remain an open challenge for all frameworks.

(2) HyPER achieves the highest overall success rate (60.8%) and the lowest mean collision count of the four evaluated frameworks, significantly outperforms both standalone baselines in success rate, and is the only framework that combines reliable detection of cliff edges with traversal of steep but passable slopes. Large pits remain challenging for all evaluated frameworks, which identifies sloped negative obstacles as the main open problem for safe subterranean navigation.

(3) Our comparative experiments show that HyPER achieves a higher overall success rate than the baseline STEP framework and that, unlike STEP, it traverses steep but passable slopes while still detecting cliff edges as hazards.

items.examiner_comment: The failure mode in the Hole environment is not fully explored, and the fusion seems to make the combination worse, which is significant. In the most safety-critical experiment the proposed approach made the outcome significantly worse, and the explanation, while going towards it, does not directly address the problem.
items.response: We agree that the original explanation was insufficient and have replaced it with an analysis of the three mechanisms behind this failure: point-wise slope labels cannot represent a drop-off; sparse returns from the embankments prevent the occlusion rule from flagging the pit; and the 70° slope limit underestimates the sliding risk of descents. We respectfully note, however, that the fusion does not make the outcome worse: every framework fails here, and HyPER has the lowest flip-over rate (80%, compared with 90–95%). Its higher mean collision count is driven by a single run, which accounts for more than half of its collisions in this environment. The previous bolding of Table 5.5 highlighted the worst values and may have given a different impression, so we have corrected it. We also propose four changes to address the failure.
items.change_made: Rewrote the Hole analysis in Section 5.3. Rewrote the negative-obstacle paragraph in Section 6.2. Corrected the bolding in the flip-over table. Updated the Hole summary in Appendix C.
items.quote_from_text:
(1) This terminal failure occurred across both the heuristic and learning-based methods, pointing to a specific limitation in the training data distribution. The deep learning models, including RandLA-Net and HyPER, fail to predict high risk for the hole's edge because they were never exposed to negative obstacles during training. In a negative obstacle scenario, there are no data points within the void itself to indicate a solid surface. Since the training dataset exclusively contained positive obstacles, such as walls and upward ramps, the network could not learn the relationship between a downward slope and an empty void. Instead, it likely misclassified the edge of the hole as a safe downward slope leading to flat ground, similar to the ramps it encountered during training. This demonstrates that without specific training data representing negative obstacles, where the absence of LiDAR returns strongly correlates with a drop-off, the model cannot learn to distinguish between a safe descent and a dangerous void, even if the slope angles appear identical at the edge.

(2) The Hole environment exposes the most critical failure mode of the current framework: a complete inability to detect negative obstacles such as pits and void edges. This failure is a direct consequence of the training data distribution, which contains only positive obstacles. In a downward-drop scenario, LiDAR beams pass through the void without returning a surface measurement. Because the network is never exposed to this pattern, where the absence of returns below the robot's current elevation indicates a hazard, it tends to misclassify pit edges as traversable descents. Two complementary solutions are under consideration. First, dedicated negative obstacle examples are included in the training set to represent scenarios where sparse or missing returns along the gravity vector are strong indicators of danger. Second, the input feature vector provided to RandLA-Net is augmented with ray-casting features that explicitly encode the expected versus actual return density along the downward direction. This provides the network with a direct signal for empty space, enabling it to distinguish between a safe downward slope and a hazardous cliff edge.

(3) Table 5.5 (flip-over rates): bold applied to the highest (worst) rates: RandLA-Net 55.0 and STEP + RandLA-Net 60.0 (Cliff), and all four Hole values (95.0, 95.0, 90.0, 80.0).
Caption: "Summary of flip-over rates (%) across all experimental environments. Arrows (↓) indicate that lower values represent superior platform stability. The results highlight the catastrophic failure of standalone learning methods in negative obstacle scenarios (Cliff), and the universal challenge posed by the Hole environment."

(4) Without specific training exposure to negative voids where LiDAR returns are absent, the systems struggle to distinguish between a safe descent and a catastrophic drop-off, often detecting the hazard only after entering a non-recoverable sliding zone.
items.revised_text_fix:
(1) Because the Hole is the most safety-critical scenario, we examine the cause of this universal failure in detail. It arises from the interaction of three limitations.

First, neither risk branch can represent a drop-off from the points at its edge. Our geometric labelling pipeline (Section 4.3.2) assigns each point a risk class from its own local surface normal. Points on the lip of a pit lie on near-level ground and therefore receive low-risk labels, while the empty space beyond the lip contains no points and receives no label at all. Although our training data includes drives off cliff edges (Section 4.3), the labels from those runs encode the same pattern, so RandLA-Net learns to treat level ground as safe regardless of what lies beyond it. Similarly, the STEP branch computes step and slope risk only from neighbouring cells that contain data, so a lip bordering an unobserved region also appears level.

Second, the visibility-aware occlusion handling does not activate reliably at the pit. In the Cliff environment, the vertical drop produces a contiguous region with no LiDAR returns inside the scanning annulus; these cells satisfy the void condition |P_w,l| = 0 and receive the maximum risk, which explains HyPER's success there. The pit, by contrast, is bounded by steep but visible embankments that return sparse points. Because we accumulate points over successive scans, a cell that receives even a single return is removed from the void set V. The fusion equation instead scores such cells with low confidence, but the uncertainty penalty adds at most λ = 15 on the 0–50 scale, below the 90% threshold that triggers the exploration strategy and the proximity inflation, so sparsely observed cells inside the pit are treated as moderate rather than prohibitive risk.

Third, the slope scale underestimates the danger of the embankments. Both the STEP slope risk and our labelling pipeline normalise slope by θ_max = 70°, so an embankment of, for example, 35° receives a risk of only 0.5 (class 25). Descending such a slope is nevertheless unrecoverable, because the robot slides into the pit, and we deliberately exclude slippage from the heuristic risk model (Section 4.4.1). All four frameworks therefore plan across the upper part of the embankment and enter the sliding zone before sensor evidence of the pit floor becomes available.

Within this common failure, the weighted fusion does not worsen the outcome. HyPER records the lowest flip-over rate in the Hole environment (80%, compared with 90–95% for the baselines, Table 5.5); its remaining four runs end without a tip-over, through immobilisation or by reaching the iteration limit. Its higher mean collision count (41.10, compared with 1.90 for Simple Fusion) is driven by a single run: with a standard deviation of 128.51 over 20 runs, one run must account for more than half of the total, and the same pattern explains the high means of STEP and RandLA-Net. Four changes would address the mechanisms identified above: (i) treating unobserved neighbours as maximum risk in the step and slope computation; (ii) replacing the binary void test |P_w,l| = 0 with a test on the ratio of observed to expected returns at the cell's range; (iii) increasing λ so that cells with near-zero confidence approach the high-risk threshold; and (iv) using a separate, lower slope limit for descents.

(2) The Hole environment exposes the most critical failure mode of the current framework: the detection of sloped negative obstacles such as pits. Building on the analysis in Section 5.3, we propose as future work to (i) extend the labelling pipeline so that points adjacent to unobserved space below the local ground level receive high-risk labels, using ray casting to compare expected and actual returns along each beam; (ii) augment the RandLA-Net input features with this expected-versus-actual return density, giving the network a direct signal for empty space; (iii) replace the binary void test in the occlusion handling with a density-ratio test and increase the uncertainty penalty for near-zero confidence; and (iv) introduce a direction-dependent slope limit that penalises descents more heavily than ascents. The virtual surfaces of Hines et al. [2020], developed for the DARPA SubT Challenge, provide a promising complement to these changes.

(3) Table 5.5: bold now marks the lowest rate in each environment where the methods differ: STEP and HyPER 0.0 (Cliff); STEP, RandLA-Net and HyPER 0.0 (Multi-Ramp); RandLA-Net 0.0 (Obstacles Ramp); HyPER 80.0 (Hole).
Caption: "Flip-over rates (%) per environment (20 runs each). Bold marks the lowest rate in each environment where the methods differ."

(4) All frameworks detect the pit only after entering a non-recoverable sliding zone; Section 5.3 analyses the causes.

items.examiner_comment: The argument for labelling data from the simulator is well reasoned; however, how this algorithm would be trained and labelled with real subterranean data is not fully explored.
items.response: We agree and have added a paragraph to Future Work describing how HyPER would be trained on real subterranean data: teleoperated collection with LiDAR-inertial registration, cleaning of real-sensor artefacts, geometric labelling with platform-specific limits, and additional sources of hazard labels, since deliberate failures cannot be repeated on hardware. The simulation-trained network would then be fine-tuned on the real data.
items.change_made: Added a paragraph to Section 6.2 (Future Work).
items.quote_from_text: (No existing text replaced — new paragraph inserted after the first paragraph of Section 6.2, which ends '…without requiring exhaustive manual annotation.')
items.revised_text_fix: Our geometric labelling pipeline is developed on simulated data, but its main steps require only point coordinates and do not depend on the simulator. We envisage training HyPER on real subterranean data in four stages. First, we would collect LiDAR data by teleoperating the physical robot through representative tunnels and caves, registering the scans with LiDAR-inertial odometry. Second, we would remove artefacts absent from simulation, such as dust returns, multipath reflections and isolated outliers, before estimating surface normals. Third, we would generate the slope-based labels with θ_max set to the measured limits of the physical platform. Fourth, because the deliberate failures used in simulation, such as driving off cliff edges, cannot be repeated with real hardware, labels for dangerous regions would come from other sources: ray-cast labels for points adjacent to unobserved space below ground level (proposed in the next paragraph), a small manually annotated set of hazardous regions, combined with the proprioceptive label correction described above. We would then fine-tune the simulation-trained network on this real dataset, which we expect to require far fewer labelled scans than training from scratch. Public subterranean datasets such as SubT-MRS [Zhao et al. 2024] could provide additional real point clouds for this training.
